name: half-sync-half-async
context: The Half-Sync/Half-Async pattern addresses the tension between concurrent programming simplicity and execution efficiency in complex software systems. Higher-level business logic benefits from synchronous processing models (blocking I/O, straightforward control flow), while lower-level I/O operations (interrupts, network events) require asynchronous processing for optimal performance. This pattern integrates both approaches through a queueing layer that mediates communication between the synchronous and asynchronous task layers.
benefits: Simplified programming model for business logic using synchronous operations
High performance through efficient non-blocking I/O at lower levels
Strong decoupling between processing layers with well-defined boundaries
Horizontal scalability via multiple sync workers processing queued tasks
Fast responsiveness with immediate acknowledgment while processing continues
Multi-processor efficiency with simplified synchronous I/O programming
Centralized communication through queueing layer mediation
tradeoffs: Boundary-crossing penalty from context switching and synchronization overhead
Increased debugging complexity due to asynchronous callbacks
Queue management burden including flow control and backpressure
Data copying overhead from protection domain crossings
Concurrency control complexity for serialize access to shared resources
Asynchronous I/O limitations for higher-level tasks depending on framework
use_cases: Web API with async offload for logging, notifications, and emails
E-commerce checkout with sync payment and async shipping/confirmation
Data pipeline ingestion with sync acknowledgment and async processing
Microservices enrichment with sync core logic and async external calls
Document processing with sync acceptance and async heavy computation
Database operations with sync queries and async replication/backup
avoid_when: Workloads are purely synchronous with no benefit from async offload
Only simple request-response without long-running tasks
Low latency is critical and boundary-crossing overhead cannot be tolerated
Limited threading capability or single-threaded runtime
Team lacks experience with concurrent programming and queue management
System is small enough that complexity outweighs benefits
component_types: Async Event Handler/Dispatcher: Receives requests non-blocking, enqueues for processing. Immediately returns control to caller
Message Queue/Buffer: Decouples async receiver from sync processing with bounded capacity. Provides thread-safe buffering
Sync Worker Thread Pool: Fixed-size pool processing queued tasks with blocking I/O. Executes long-running operations
Callback/Completion Handler: Notifies clients when processing completes. Handles result delivery and error propagation
Flow Control Manager: Implements backpressure, rate limiting, and adaptive throttling to prevent overwhelm
Queue Monitor: Tracks queue depth, latency, and health metrics for observability and alerting
technology_stack: Python: asyncio, queue.Queue, Celery, FastAPI with background tasks
Node.js: Event loop, RabbitMQ, Kafka client
Message Queues: RabbitMQ, Apache Kafka, Redis Streams
anti_patterns: Shared database between layers creating tight coupling
Blocking the async layer instead of delegating to sync workers
Unbounded queues causing memory exhaustion risk
Ignoring backpressure leading to sync layer overwhelm
Complex nested callbacks without structure causing callback hell
design_principles: Layer Isolation: Synchronous and asynchronous layers must only communicate through the queueing layer
Non-Blocking Async: Async handlers must never block—they enqueue and return immediately
Bounded Queues: Use bounded queues with backpressure to prevent memory exhaustion
Fixed Worker Pool: Sync workers should use a fixed-size thread pool to control resource usage
Clear Responsibility Division: Sync layer handles business logic; async layer handles I/O events
Flow Control: Implement backpressure mechanisms to prevent sync layer overwhelm
best_practices: Queue Sizing: Size queues based on expected load and acceptable latency; monitor for saturation
Thread Pool Tuning: Adjust worker pool size based on workload characteristics (CPU vs I/O bound)
Backpressure Implementation: Use flow control to regulate task submission when workers are saturated
Error Handling: Implement retry mechanisms and dead letter queues for failed processing
Monitoring: Add metrics for queue depth, processing latency, worker utilization, and rejection rates
Graceful Degradation: Implement circuit breakers when downstream services fail
Callback Management: Use structured callback patterns to avoid callback hell; consider futures/promises
